title: The FaaS Execution Model: Cold Starts & Concurrency
summary: The mechanics that make serverless performance characteristics different from a warm server — cold starts, concurrency limits, and execution time caps.

slides.markdown:
The FaaS execution model explains why a serverless function's latency isn't constant — the same code can respond in 5ms or 800ms depending on whether an execution environment already exists.

- **Cold vs warm** starts are the single biggest source of serverless latency variance.
- **Concurrency** and **execution time limits** are the platform's guardrails, not tuning knobs you control directly.

A **cold start** provisions a fresh environment before code runs: allocate a sandbox, init the runtime, load dependencies, then execute. A **warm start** skips straight to execution, reusing a live environment.

![Cold start vs warm start timeline](assets/cold-start-vs-warm-start.svg)

The gap is almost entirely setup, not your code — a 10ms handler can still take 800ms end-to-end when cold.

assets.alt: Cold start vs warm start timeline

slides.markdown:
A cold start's time is spent before your handler ever runs: **provisioning** a sandbox (allocating compute for the invocation), **initializing the runtime** (starting the language VM — a JVM is notably slower here than a lightweight interpreter), and **loading your package** (unzipping and importing every dependency you bundled, even ones a given invocation doesn't use).

A function with 200MB of dependencies and a heavyweight runtime can spend most of its cold-start time in these three steps, before a single line of your code executes.

Three levers reliably shrink cold-start time. **Smaller packages** — trim unused dependencies so there's less to load. **Lighter runtimes** — a fast-starting interpreted language beats a JVM-based one for pure cold-start latency. **Provisioned concurrency** — pay to keep a set number of environments pre-initialized and warm at all times, trading pay-per-use savings for predictable, near-zero cold starts on that slice of traffic.

None of these are free — provisioned concurrency in particular re-introduces a standing cost closer to an always-on server.

The platform decides how many invocations of your function run in parallel — each concurrent invocation gets its own execution environment, and the platform scales that number up automatically as events arrive. This is the mechanism behind serverless's "scales instantly" promise: no autoscaling group to configure.

But it isn't unlimited. Every platform enforces a **concurrency limit** — a cap on simultaneous executions per function or account — past which further invocations queue or are throttled, which matters enormously for downstream systems with their own connection limits.

Every FaaS platform caps how long a single invocation may run — commonly minutes, not hours. This isn't an arbitrary restriction: it reflects the model's assumption that a function does one bounded unit of work per event, not a long-lived job.

Work that genuinely takes longer — a multi-hour video transcode, a batch ETL job — doesn't fit the model and needs a different compute type (a container or VM), or must be broken into a chain of shorter, resumable steps.

slides.subTitle: Comparing cold-start latency across runtimes
slides.markdown:
| Runtime choice | Typical cold start | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Lightweight interpreted | ~100-300ms | Small runtime binary, fast interpreter startup |
| JVM-based | ~800ms-2s+ | Class loading and JIT warm-up before code runs |

**How to decide:** for latency-sensitive, frequently-cold endpoints (a user-facing API called sporadically), the lighter runtime's cold-start difference is often decisive; for steady, high-throughput functions that stay warm, the gap barely matters.

slides.subTitle: Benchmarking only warm invocations
slides.markdown:
The wrong belief: a load test showing consistently fast response times means the function performs well in production. If the test keeps the function warm — steady traffic, no gaps — it never measures a cold start at all, and cold starts are exactly what real, bursty user traffic triggers.

The correct model: deliberately test after an idle period, and track the cold-start tail (p99, not just average) separately from warm-invocation latency — they're different characteristics with different causes.

slides.subTitle: A concurrency limit causing throttling under a traffic spike
slides.markdown:
A function's account-level concurrency limit is set to 1,000. A marketing push drives a spike to 4,000 simultaneous invocations. The platform runs the first 1,000 normally; the rest are either **queued** (for async triggers like a queue, which tolerate delay) or **throttled with an error** (for synchronous triggers like HTTP, which can't wait indefinitely) — the caller sees 429s or timeouts exactly at the moment traffic is highest.

The fix isn't code — it's requesting a concurrency limit increase ahead of the known spike, and adding a **reserved concurrency** floor for the function so a burst elsewhere in the account can't starve it. This is why capacity planning for serverless means planning concurrency headroom, not server count.
